06 Substance use and other · class card

Substance use and cessation

naltrexone · acamprosate · disulfiram · buprenorphine · methadone · varenicline · nicotine replacement

Key point
  • Buprenorphine: binds tighter than a full agonist, activates less if dosed before withdrawal signs, it displaces the full agonist precipitated withdrawal
  • Naltrexone: for alcohol it can start while still drinking; for opioids only after withdrawal is complete; avoid with liver disease, never with acute hepatitis or liver failure
  • Methadone: long-acting full agonist accumulates; QT prolongation; CYP3A4 (cytochrome P450 3A4) inhibitors raise the level opioid toxicity
  • Varenicline is the most effective single smoking drug, then combination nicotine replacement, then bupropion
Drugs

Naltrexone Vivitrol (monthly injection): mu-opioid antagonist

Acamprosate: glutamate modulator

Disulfiram: a deterrent

Buprenorphine, with naloxone as Suboxone: partial mu agonist

Methadone Methadose: long-acting full agonist

Varenicline Chantix: nicotinic partial agonist

Nicotine replacement: NicoDerm CQ (patch), gum or lozenge Nicorette for cravings; the patch keeps a steady level Nicotine replacementIn practice: combined nicotine forms work about as well as varenicline.

Mechanism

Naltrexone: mu receptor blocked opioid euphoria blocked; less craving and fewer heavy drinking days Naloxone or naltrexoneNaloxone treats toxicity; naltrexone prevents relapse.

Acamprosate: glutamate modulated less craving once abstinent

Disulfiram: acetaldehyde dehydrogenase blocked acetaldehyde builds after a drink Disulfiram reactionThink of the reaction as a really bad hangover: acetaldehyde causes hangover symptoms.

Buprenorphine: high affinity, low efficacy a ceiling on respiratory depression

Naloxone in the combination: inactive under the tongue; injected, it precipitates withdrawal deters misuse

Methadone: long half-life steady receptor activation no withdrawal, less craving Methadone accumulationIt can build up faster than it is cleared.

Varenicline: nicotinic partial agonist less withdrawal and craving Varenicline receptorThe alpha-4 beta-2 nicotinic receptor (label). It also partly blocks the effects of nicotine. Nicotine withdrawal brings irritability, anxiety, restlessness and poor concentration.

Uses

Alcohol use disorder: naltrexone or acamprosate first line, acamprosate preferred with liver disease or opioid use; disulfiram second line; alongside psychosocial treatment

Opioid use disorder: buprenorphine or methadone maintenance first line, often long term; long-acting naltrexone after withdrawal, for mild disorder Opioid maintenanceWhen maintenance is going well, continue it; in a highly motivated patient a slow taper may be tried, with close watch for relapse.

Opioid use disorder in pregnancy: methadone or buprenorphine PregnancyBetter maternal and newborn outcomes than abstinence.

Quitting smoking: varenicline, nicotine replacement and bupropion are all first line

Adverse effects

Naltrexone: hepatotoxicity; precipitated withdrawal with opioids on board

Acamprosate: diarrhea; kidney-cleared, so avoid with significant impairment Acamprosate labelIn practice: the label contraindicates it at a creatinine clearance of 30 mL/min or less.

Disulfiram: reaction with any alcohol (see the disulfiram reaction row below); not in pregnancy or cardiac decompensation Disulfiram labelHepatitis, sometimes fatal, may develop even after months; optic and peripheral neuritis may occur; contraindicated with psychosis or severe myocardial disease. Never given to an intoxicated patient or without the patient knowing.

Methadone: QT prolongation, torsades de pointes; accumulation and overdose

Varenicline: nausea, headaches, insomnia, abnormal dreams, depressed mood Varenicline labelNausea and sleep complaints lead. New or worsening seizures were seen in people taking it; severe kidney impairment starts a lower dose.

Nicotine replacement: angina is not a contraindication; caution with serious angina or within 2 weeks of a myocardial infarction Nicotine replacement and anginaUse cautiously with certain cardiovascular risks; most data suggest it is safe.

Precipitated withdrawalRapid, severe withdrawal after a first buprenorphine or naltrexone dose with a full agonist on board

If opioid withdrawal signs are not yet present, choose waiting, then buprenorphine once withdrawal signs appear.

Disulfiram reactionFlushing within minutes of a drink, then throbbing headache, tachycardia, sweating and nausea Severe reactionLarge amounts add vomiting and hypotension; the reaction can last up to 3 hours.

If drinking has not stopped, choose naltrexone; disulfiram needs abstinence.

Methadone toxicitySedation, small pupils and slow breathing during titration or after a CYP3A4 inhibitor joins methadone

If breathing slows on methadone, choose naloxone; methadone outlasts a dose, so some need an infusion and admission.

Interactions, by result
Combined withResultRule
Methadone with a CYP3A4 inhibitor CYP3A4 inhibitorsAn azole, clarithromycin, ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine or cimetidine.Methadone level up: opioid toxicityWatch for sedation and slow breathing
Methadone with a benzodiazepine or other sedativeCan cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, deathOnly when alternatives are inadequate
Disulfiram with a drink, cough syrup or elixirDisulfiram reactionNo alcohol in any form
Naltrexone with opioidsPrecipitated withdrawalNot together
Quitting smoking on clozapineClozapine level rises Clozapine and smokingTobacco smoke induces cytochrome P450 1A2; the induction fades after quitting. Consider a lower clozapine dose
Monitoring
WhenCheckWhy
Methadone start and titrationElectrocardiogram (ECG) for the QT intervalA life-threatening arrhythmia risk
Methadone use in questionSpecialized urine testingMethadone is not detected the usual way
On disulfiramLiver tests at baseline and at 10 to 14 daysA sometimes fatal organ injury that may develop even after months
Varenicline or bupropionMood and behaviorEvents reported after marketing Label warningIn practice: no causal link was confirmed in trials, and the boxed warning was removed.
Acute pain on methadone or buprenorphineKeep the maintenance dose; add opioid analgesiaTreat pain as for any patient
Where the choice is made

Intoxication, withdrawal and overdose, naloxone included

Bupropion for quitting smoking

Readiness to change and motivational interviewing

Practice
  1. 44-year-old man with alcohol use disorder wants to cut down drinks 8 beers daily; strong cravings takes no opioids or other drugs AST 38 U/L · ALT 30 U/L · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → Naltrexone → still drinking with cravings, no opioids and a healthy liver: naltrexone can start now; disulfiram is for abstinent patients, and chlordiazepoxide treats withdrawal, not the use disorder
  2. 51-year-old woman with alcohol use disorder and cirrhosis abstinent 3 weeks since a hospital stay cravings; afraid she will relapse; no opioids or tobacco creatinine 0.8 mg/dL · albumin 3.0 g/dL → Acamprosate → abstinent with liver disease: acamprosate is excreted mostly unchanged by the kidneys and is safe for the liver; naltrexone is contraindicated with liver disease, and disulfiram is second line
  3. 29-year-old man with opioid use disorder wants buprenorphine today last used heroin 3 hours ago calm; no yawning, sweating or goose flesh pupils 3 mm · HR 78/min · BP 124/78 mm Hg → Wait for withdrawal signs, then give buprenorphine → heroin is still on board and withdrawal has not begun: buprenorphine now would displace it and precipitate withdrawal, so the first dose waits for withdrawal signs; naltrexone needs a completed withdrawal
  4. 26-year-old woman, 11 weeks pregnant, injects heroin daily wants to stop for the baby asks to come off all opioids now HR 84/min · BP 116/72 mm Hg · urine screen positive for opiates → Buprenorphine maintenance → opioid use disorder in pregnancy: methadone or buprenorphine maintenance brings better maternal and neonatal outcomes than abstinence; withdrawal alone risks relapse, and naltrexone needs a completed withdrawal
  5. 47-year-old man on methadone maintenance for 2 years started clarithromycin 4 days ago for pneumonia now drowsy and hard to rouse; no new drug use RR 8/min · pupils 2 mm · oxygen saturation 89% → Methadone toxicity → clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and raises the methadone level: sedation, small pupils and slow breathing are opioid toxicity; withdrawal brings dilated pupils, yawning and sweating
  6. 38-year-old woman with opioid use disorder started on methadone the dose is being raised over several weeks no other medicines; no known heart disease HR 72/min · BP 118/76 mm Hg · alert, not sedated → ECG during titration → methadone prolongs the QTc and can cause torsades de pointes, so ECGs are monitored during initiation and titration; liver injury is the naltrexone concern, and kidney function the acamprosate one
  7. 52-year-old man smokes 1 pack a day and wants to quit asks for the single most effective medicine no seizures, eating disorder or psychiatric illness BP 132/84 mm Hg · HR 76/min → Varenicline → varenicline is the most effective single drug; combination nicotine replacement comes next and bupropion last; a single nicotine product is weaker than combined products
  8. 45-year-old woman taking varenicline for 3 weeks to quit smoking nausea and vivid dreams she cannot tolerate wants another medicine to stay off cigarettes BP 124/80 mm Hg · HR 70/min → Nicotine patch plus nicotine gum → varenicline side effects not tolerated: combination nicotine replacement, a patch for a steady level plus gum for cravings; combined products beat a single one, and acamprosate is an alcohol relapse drug
